messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] EzPlot2 y-axis range
messages.body_plain:
ezPlot/ezPlot2 generate ggplot2 objects, so you can use ggplot2's scale_y_continuous() function, as in:

my_plot = ezPlot2(...)

my_plot + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-1,1))

Cheers,

Mike

messages.subject: Re: anova with log-transformed values?
messages.body_plain:
No. It wouldn't. When you compare means on the log scale you are really comparing geometric means (which are also the medians of a lognormal distribution). There is nothing wrong with this. It is a different quantity than the arithmetic mean. The real question is what quantity is of interest to you. If either of interest (e.g., you are just interested in central tendency in general) you just need to make sure that you don't report or misinterpret the quantity.

Thom

messages.subject: getting started
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I don't have a lot of experience with mixed models in R but it seems like this package is a great place to start.  I was wondering if anyone has any pointers to examples for me to get started.  I apologize if this is already published somewhere obvious... I did search the archives for words like "introduction."

Many thanks,
Mike
messages.body_snippet: Hi, I don't have a lot of experience with mixed models in R but it seems like this package is a great place to start.  I was wondering if anyone has any pointers to examples for me to get started.  I

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] getting started
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

I haven't written a detailed introduction with examples yet. You can read up on mixed effects models by checking out chapter 12 of Baayen's "Analyzing Linguistic Data" (http://www.ualberta.ca/~baayen/publications/baayenCUPstats.pdf) and Bates' in progress text (http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org/lMMwR/).

In the meantime, here's a general description of the approach that ezMixed() takes:

The ezMixed() function automates the process of evaluating the evidence for fixed effects in a mixed effects modelling context. It permits multiple (non-nested) random effects and can use generalized additive modelling to characterize possibly-non-linear effects associated with continuous fixed effects variables. For each fixed effect of interest, it will compute two models, a restricted model where the effect of interest is restricted to zero (no effect), and an unrestricted model where the effect of interest is estimated from the data. The likelihood of these two models are then compared, using AIC to correct for the increased complexity of the unrestricted model and presenting the resulting corrected likelihood ratio on the log-base-2 scale, where the value can be referred to in terms of "bits of evidence". For effects that have reasonable evidence (I usually use >3 bits as a rule of thumb when I don't have strong prior expectations), the nature of the effects can be visualized using the ezPredict() and ezPlot2() functions.

Limitations:
- ezMixed can't evaluate the evidence for random effects. While the ezMixed approach (likelihood ratio comparing a restricted vs unrestricted model) should work fine to achieve this, I don't tend to need this in my own research, so I haven't gotten around to including it.
- ezMixed can only model simple random effects on intercepts. More complicated models involving variability in the manifestation of fixed effects across levels of a random effect are not possible. For simple scenarios, the likelihood ratio approach could reasonably work, but things get complicated when you have multiple fixed effects and it became too much of a headache to code. I have run simulations exploring the consequences of this simplification, and, as one might expect, it seems that failing to account for such extra sources of variance when they exist reduce the evidence associated with the overall evaluation of the fixed effect under consideration.
- ezMixed doesn't do any assumption checking. You should check the residuals of the fitted models to ensure they meet the normalilty assumption

Cheers,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

messages.subject: Planned contrasts with ezANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Can ezANOVA do planned contrasts? If so, how? If not, is there some way to do the contrasts using the output of ezANOVA?

Here's my model for reference:

options(contrasts=c("contr.sum","contr.poly"))
ezANOVA( data=D, dv=.(change), wid=.(subjid), within=.(schema), between=.(training,prevexp), type=3 )

change ranges from -1.0 to 1.0. schema has 5 levels. prevexp has two levels - high or low. training has 3 levels, let's say A, B, and C. I get a significant interaction of training with prevexp. I have a priori reasons to group training B and C together, and if I recode training with two levels, i.e. A vs B/C, I still get the above interaction with prevexp. What I'd like to do is put all of this into a single analysis that will say

1. whether there's an interaction of A vs. B/C, or A vs. B vs. C, with prevexp? (I am fine posing this question in either of these two ways, whichever works better.)
2. whether A differs from B/C at each level of prevexp?
3. whether B differs from C at each level of prevexp?

Hope this is clear. If anyone wants to give guidance on the stats aspect of this it would be very helpful, but I'm mainly asking about how to do the above with ez. Thanks in advance!

designs are in a later chapter).

See

http://seriousstats.wordpress.com/2012/03/23/serious-stats-companion-web-site-now-live/

That said I'd be interested to know about options for planned contrasts in ezANOVA.

Thom

messages.body_plain:
My sincere apologies for failing to reply earlier.

The problem with your example is that ezPredict wants to obtain predictions for every combination of every level of every predictor in the model, which can blow up when you have a continuous predictor in the mix with lots of levels. To constain things, set the value of the "numeric_res" argument to something like 10:

    rt_preds = ezPredict(
        fit = rt_fit

        , numeric_res = 10
    )
